name: CUSP42 Atlas
description: A curated gateway for AI, institutional risk, political economy, multi-agent reasoning, and scenario analysis. Machine-readable companion to https://cusp42.com/atlas.html
publisher: CUSP42 Labs (independent research and product studio)

resources.name: Stanford HAI AI Index
resources.summary: Annual, data-driven report from the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI tracking AI's technical progress, economic influence, and societal impact.
resources.whyItMatters: One of the few durable, self-updating baselines for claims about where AI actually is.
resources.bestFor: Grounding AI-and-society arguments in shared data before debating interpretations.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A common evidence base for scenario baselines and structured-debate prompts.

resources.name: MIT Stone Center on Inequality and Shaping the Future of Work
resources.summary: MIT research center co-directed by Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, and Simon Johnson, studying how technology reshapes labor markets, inequality, and institutions.
resources.whyItMatters: The most rigorous economics program on automation, labor absorption, and the institutional direction of technological change.
resources.bestFor: Researchers working on AI, labor, and distribution.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Anchors CUSP42's labor-absorption and institutional-adaptation questions in serious scholarship.

resources.name: OECD.AI Policy Observatory
resources.summary: The OECD's living portal of national AI policies, governance initiatives, and near-real-time indicators on AI research, jobs, skills, and investment.
resources.whyItMatters: Tracks how states actually respond to AI rather than what commentators predict they will do.
resources.bestFor: Policy professionals comparing governance approaches across jurisdictions.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A source of real institutional responses to feed scenario and stress-pathway thinking.

resources.name: Anthropic Economic Index
resources.summary: Recurring reports and open data tracking how AI assistants are actually used across occupations, tasks, and geographies.
resources.whyItMatters: Usage-based evidence on AI's penetration into real work, available ahead of official labor statistics.
resources.bestFor: Analysts who want adoption data rather than adoption anecdotes.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Empirical input for CUSP42's labor and distribution scenarios.
resources.limitation: Single-provider data: reflects one company's user base and methodology.

resources.name: Epoch AI
resources.summary: Research group publishing data and analysis on compute, frontier models, hardware, data centers, and the economics of AI development.
resources.whyItMatters: Compute, energy, and capital are the physical substrate of AI power; Epoch measures them instead of speculating about them.
resources.bestFor: Understanding infrastructure, gatekeeping, and concentration questions with numbers.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Grounds 'compute as institutional power' arguments in measurable trends.

resources.name: IMF Global Financial Stability Report
resources.summary: The IMF's twice-yearly assessment of global financial stability risks; recent editions analyze AI's implications for capital markets and financial intermediation.
resources.whyItMatters: The canonical recurring map of how new shocks propagate through balance sheets, credit, and liquidity systems.
resources.bestFor: Risk professionals borrowing macro-financial stress logic for AI questions.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A model for how CUSP42 thinks about technology shocks becoming institutional events.

resources.name: FSB: Monitoring Adoption of Artificial Intelligence and Related Vulnerabilities in the Financial Sector
resources.summary: Financial Stability Board work on how AI adoption creates monitorable vulnerabilities across the financial system.
resources.whyItMatters: Shows how a global standard-setter converts 'AI risk' talk into concrete monitoring channels.
resources.bestFor: Translating AI concerns into supervisory and systemic-risk language.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A working template for CUSP42's AI-society transmission-chain thinking.

resources.name: Bank of England — Financial Stability in Focus: Artificial intelligence in the financial system
resources.summary: A central bank's structured assessment of how AI could affect financial stability, from operational dependence on few providers to correlated model behavior.
resources.whyItMatters: One of the clearest official articulations of AI as a systemic risk rather than a firm-level technology issue.
resources.bestFor: Concrete, practitioner-written examples of AI stress pathways.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A reference case for the institutional stress-pathway method.

resources.name: Bank for International Settlements (BIS)
resources.summary: The central bank of central banks; its research, bulletins, and Annual Economic Report increasingly cover AI, money, and financial infrastructure.
resources.whyItMatters: Long-horizon, institution-first analysis with unusual seriousness about technology and its monetary consequences.
resources.bestFor: Economists and policy thinkers who want depth over news cycles.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Supplies the institutional vocabulary CUSP42 tries to extend beyond finance.

resources.name: RAND Corporation
resources.summary: One of the largest policy research institutions and the original home of scenario methods; publishes extensively on AI, security, and long-range futures.
resources.whyItMatters: Scenario analysis as a discipline largely descends from RAND's work.
resources.bestFor: Deep policy-grade studies on futures, risk, and emerging technology.
resources.cusp42Relevance: The methodological ancestor of CUSP42's scenario-room ambitions.

resources.name: OECD Strategic Foresight
resources.summary: The OECD's program and toolkit for embedding strategic foresight into public policy.
resources.whyItMatters: A durable, practitioner-tested foresight methodology maintained by an institution rather than a consultancy trend.
resources.bestFor: Anyone building scenario and anticipation capability inside organizations.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Framework input for the CUSP42 Scenario Method.

resources.name: Shell Scenarios
resources.summary: Fifty years of published scenario practice, from the scenarios that anticipated the 1970s oil shocks to today's energy-security scenarios.
resources.whyItMatters: The longest-running demonstration that scenarios are for decisions under uncertainty, not predictions.
resources.bestFor: Learning how scenario narratives are actually constructed, named, and used by leadership.
resources.cusp42Relevance: The canonical example of 'explore paths, don't collapse to one prediction.'
resources.limitation: Written from an energy company's vantage point; read for method, not as a neutral forecast.

resources.name: NGFS Scenarios Portal
resources.summary: Climate scenarios built by a network of central banks and supervisors for financial stress testing, updated on a regular cycle.
resources.whyItMatters: The best current example of turning a slow, civilizational-scale shock into quantified institutional stress scenarios — a direct analogy for AI.
resources.bestFor: Risk professionals who want a template for scenario frameworks institutions could actually run.
resources.cusp42Relevance: The closest existing analogue to what an AI institutional-stress framework could look like.

resources.name: Metaculus
resources.summary: A long-running forecasting community that aggregates probabilistic predictions on science, technology, and AI questions, with public track records.
resources.whyItMatters: Keeps foresight honest by attaching probabilities and accountability to claims about the future.
resources.bestFor: Calibrating your own uncertainty against a serious forecasting crowd.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A live complement to scenario work: scenarios structure the possibility space, forecasts weight it.

resources.name: AI Safety via Debate (Irving, Christiano & Amodei, 2018)
resources.summary: The foundational proposal for using structured debate between AI systems, judged by humans, to surface truth on questions too hard to judge directly.
resources.whyItMatters: The intellectual root of debate-as-oversight and much of today's structured-disagreement work.
resources.bestFor: Understanding why disagreement between models is a feature, not a bug.
resources.cusp42Relevance: The theoretical ancestor of Consensus Room.

resources.name: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate (Du et al., 2023)
resources.summary: Empirical demonstration that multiple language-model instances proposing and debating answers over rounds improves factuality and reasoning.
resources.whyItMatters: The key evidence that multi-model debate measurably reduces hallucination and reasoning errors.
resources.bestFor: Builders who want the empirical case for plural reasoning workflows.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A direct evidence base for the Consensus Room design.

resources.name: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (Zheng et al., 2023)
resources.summary: The reference work on using strong models as judges of other models, documenting where LLM judges agree with humans and where they systematically fail.
resources.whyItMatters: Any workflow that lets one model grade another inherits the biases documented here.
resources.bestFor: Designing evaluation and adjudication steps in multi-agent workflows.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Informs why CUSP42 tools treat 'judge' roles skeptically and keep disagreement visible.
resources.limitation: Judge models and benchmarks evolve quickly; read it for the failure modes, not the leaderboard.

resources.name: Microsoft AutoGen
resources.summary: A widely used open-source framework for building multi-agent LLM applications, conversation patterns, and agent orchestration.
resources.whyItMatters: One of the most influential codebases for making agents talk to, review, and challenge each other.
resources.bestFor: Builders prototyping multi-agent debate and review workflows in code.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A practical playground for the patterns CUSP42 packages for non-developers.
resources.limitation: Now in maintenance mode; Microsoft's successor is Agent Framework. Read AutoGen for the patterns.

resources.name: Consensus Room (CUSP42)
resources.summary: CUSP42's browser extension for running one question across multiple AI models, with round-based debate, model comparison, voting, and a consensus report.
resources.whyItMatters: Turns multi-agent debate research into a workflow anyone can run in a browser, without writing code.
resources.bestFor: Researchers and analysts who want structured disagreement on real questions today.
resources.cusp42Relevance: The first operational CUSP42 product. The Atlas provides the map; Consensus Room provides the debate room.

resources.name: Semantic Scholar
resources.summary: AI-powered academic search engine from the Allen Institute for AI, with open APIs and citation graphs across hundreds of millions of papers.
resources.whyItMatters: Durable, non-commercial infrastructure for literature discovery, citation checking, and building research corpora.
resources.bestFor: Literature review and citation verification at scale.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A baseline evidence layer for AI-assisted research workflows.

resources.name: arXiv
resources.summary: The canonical open preprint repository where most AI research first appears, maintained since 1991.
resources.whyItMatters: Reading primary sources beats reading commentary about them; most AI claims can be traced to an arXiv page.
resources.bestFor: Going straight to the papers behind AI claims and tracking new work by topic.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Where most of the paper entries in this Atlas live.

resources.name: Zotero
resources.summary: Free, open-source reference manager for collecting, organizing, annotating, and citing research.
resources.whyItMatters: A local-first, user-owned research memory that has outlasted many commercial rivals.
resources.bestFor: Maintaining a durable personal research library across years and projects.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Matches CUSP42's local-first, user-owned-workflow principles.

resources.name: Elicit
resources.summary: An AI research assistant focused on literature screening, structured data extraction from papers, and systematic-review-style synthesis.
resources.whyItMatters: One of the more serious attempts at AI-assisted systematic review, rather than AI-written papers.
resources.bestFor: Structured literature triage on empirical questions.
resources.cusp42Relevance: An example of AI supporting research judgment instead of replacing it.
resources.limitation: Commercial product: verify extractions against sources and expect the feature set to change.

resources.name: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior (Park et al., 2023)
resources.summary: The Stanford 'AI town' experiment: 25 LLM agents with memory, reflection, and planning producing believable emergent social behavior.
resources.whyItMatters: The canonical demonstration that LLM agents can form a small society — the reference point for all subsequent agent-society work.
resources.bestFor: The starting paper for anyone exploring AI social simulation.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A seed for CUSP42's future simulation direction.

resources.name: Project Sid: Many-agent simulations toward AI civilization (Altera, 2024)
resources.summary: Simulations of 10 to 1000+ agents in a Minecraft world developing specialized roles, collective rules, and cultural and religious transmission.
resources.whyItMatters: Scales agent-society questions from a town to civilizational processes: specialization, laws, culture, and institutions.
resources.bestFor: Seeing what many-agent societies can and cannot yet do.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Direct inspiration for the possible Earth Social Simulator direction.

resources.name: Concordia (Google DeepMind)
resources.summary: A DeepMind library for generative agent-based modeling, using a game-master pattern to simulate agents grounded in physical, social, or digital settings.
resources.whyItMatters: Serious, maintained infrastructure for building social simulations rather than one-off demos.
resources.bestFor: Researchers who want to run agent-society experiments themselves.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A candidate substrate for future CUSP42 simulation experiments.

resources.name: LLM-Based Social Simulations Require a Boundary (2025)
resources.summary: A methodological argument for where LLM social simulations can and cannot be trusted, centered on behavioral heterogeneity and validity boundaries.
resources.whyItMatters: Guards against simulation hype: knowing the limits of the method is what makes the method usable.
resources.bestFor: Anyone tempted to read agent simulations as predictions.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Part of why CUSP42 frames simulation as scenario exploration, never prediction.

resources.name: Ollama
resources.summary: The simplest widely used way to run open-weight language models locally on your own machine, across platforms.
resources.whyItMatters: Local models are the foundation of resilient, private, offline-capable intelligence.
resources.bestFor: A first step into local-first AI without cloud dependence.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Embodies CUSP42's local-first and resilience principles.

resources.name: Kiwix
resources.summary: A nonprofit offline reader that packages Wikipedia and other reference works into compressed archives usable entirely without internet.
resources.whyItMatters: Knowledge preservation and access under degraded conditions is a civilizational resilience question, not a gadget.
resources.bestFor: Building offline knowledge bases for low-connectivity or disaster scenarios.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Pairs with local models: resilient knowledge plus resilient intelligence.

resources.name: Santa Fe Institute
resources.summary: The original home of complexity science: an independent institute founded in 1984 to study complex adaptive systems — physical, biological, economic, and social.
resources.whyItMatters: Agent-based modeling of societies and economies grew up here; its summer schools and Complexity Explorer courses remain the standard on-ramp.
resources.bestFor: Learning the complexity-science foundations underneath modern agent simulations.
resources.cusp42Relevance: The intellectual tradition CUSP42's simulation direction would build on.

resources.name: Complexity Science Hub (Vienna)
resources.summary: A European research institute applying complexity science and large-scale data to social, economic, medical, and ecological systems, backed by ten member institutions.
resources.whyItMatters: Demonstrates complexity methods applied to real policy questions: supply-chain fragility, systemic risk, social dynamics.
resources.bestFor: Researchers connecting network science and simulation to institutional questions.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A working example of simulation used for institutional stress thinking, not prediction.

resources.name: JASSS — Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation
resources.summary: The open-access, peer-reviewed journal of social simulation and artificial societies, published quarterly since 1998.
resources.whyItMatters: Twenty-five-plus years of methodology, validation debates, and worked social simulations — the field's institutional memory.
resources.bestFor: Grounding LLM-agent enthusiasm in decades of prior social-simulation scholarship.
resources.cusp42Relevance: The peer-reviewed standard any Earth Social Simulator claim would have to meet.

resources.name: NetLogo
resources.summary: The standard agent-based modeling environment from Northwestern University, with a huge library of ready-to-run social, economic, and ecological models.
resources.whyItMatters: The fastest way to actually run a society-scale model today and build intuition for emergence, tipping points, and segregation dynamics.
resources.bestFor: Hands-on learning: run Schelling segregation or epidemic models in minutes.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Proof that simple agent rules can illuminate institutional dynamics without any LLM.

resources.name: Mesa (Python agent-based modeling)
resources.summary: The leading Python library for agent-based modeling — the Python-native alternative to NetLogo, developed openly since 2015 with an active community.
resources.whyItMatters: Brings agent-based social modeling into the standard Python data ecosystem, making models analyzable and reproducible.
resources.bestFor: Builders who want programmable, data-friendly society models.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A natural bridge between classic ABM discipline and new LLM-agent experiments.

resources.name: Generative Agents — official code (Smallville)
resources.summary: The released code behind the Stanford Generative Agents paper: the 'Smallville' sandbox town where 25 LLM agents live, remember, reflect, and socialize.
resources.whyItMatters: Lets you inspect and rerun the canonical agent-society experiment rather than just reading about it.
resources.bestFor: Builders who want to study the memory-reflection-planning architecture directly.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Reference implementation for any future CUSP42 simulation prototype.

resources.name: Generative Agent Simulations of 1,000 People (Park et al., 2024)
resources.summary: Stanford follow-up that builds agents from two-hour interviews with 1,052 real individuals, replicating their survey responses with roughly 85% of human test-retest accuracy.
resources.whyItMatters: Moves agent simulation from 'believable characters' toward measured fidelity against real people — and shows exactly where fidelity ends.
resources.bestFor: Understanding what 'simulating people' can honestly claim today.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Sets the evidential bar for any social-simulation claims CUSP42 might make.

resources.name: AgentSociety (Tsinghua FIB Lab)
resources.summary: A large-scale social simulator from Tsinghua University combining LLM-driven agents with a realistic urban environment — 10,000+ agents and millions of interactions.
resources.whyItMatters: One of the most serious university-built platforms for studying social behavior, policy, and economics with LLM agents at scale.
resources.bestFor: Researchers exploring city- and society-scale LLM simulation infrastructure.
resources.cusp42Relevance: Close to the Earth Social Simulator idea in spirit: environment, institutions, and agents together.

resources.name: OASIS (CAMEL-AI)
resources.summary: An open social-media simulator scaling to one million agents, used to study information spreading, group polarization, and herd effects on X- and Reddit-like platforms.
resources.whyItMatters: Information dynamics — spread, polarization, herding — are exactly the phenomena institutions struggle to reason about; OASIS makes them experimentable.
resources.bestFor: Studying media and information-flow scenarios with many-agent experiments.
resources.cusp42Relevance: A testbed for the information-flow and legitimacy modules a future simulator would need.
